query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Augmenting standard EAM potentials with a neural network–based correction trained on ~10,000 ab initio configurations will improve the description of liquid atomic configurations in multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting, thereby reducing the thermodynamic integration path mismatch by roughly 30–40% compared to TOR-TILD’s EAM references and enabling free-energy predictions within ±5 meV/atom of ab initio results.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states at and near their melting temperatures, currently modeled using conventional EAM potentials.
generation.intervention: Implement a hybrid neural network correction for EAM potentials. The NN is trained on the residuals between standard EAM predictions and ab initio computed energies from a large dataset (~10,000 configurations) covering the liquid and solid phases.
generation.conditions: This method is applicable for high-entropy alloys (multicomponent systems) in the temperature range of approximately 0.9–1.1 times their melting temperatures (Tm), covering both the solid and liquid regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: A hybrid potential model that retains the basic EAM framework but incorporates NN corrections to better capture the diversity of atomic interactions in the ab initio liquid.
generation.mechanism: The NN learns from ab initio residuals and adjusts the EAM potential energy landscape to more accurately represent the ensemble of atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid state. This enhanced phase‐space overlap reduces the mismatch in the thermodynamic integration pathway by providing a reference energy surface closer to the target ab initio surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: The improved reference should reduce the thermodynamic integration path mismatch by approximately 30–40% relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references and yield free-energy calculations that agree with direct ab initio results to within ±5 meV/atom.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD’s conventional EAM references, which suffer from limited configurational representation in the ab initio liquid state.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected for high-entropy alloy compositions within the tested range and specifically in the high-temperature regime (0.9–1.1 Tm). The method’s performance outside these ranges is not addressed by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements may vary with the quality and diversity of the training dataset. The estimated 30–40% reduction and ±5 meV/atom agreement are based on analogous successes in elemental and binary systems and may not fully translate to the more complex high-entropy alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of free-energy thermodynamic integration (TI) calculations on high-entropy alloys in both the liquid and solid phases at temperatures between 0.9 and 1.1 Tm using both the hybrid NN-corrected EAM potentials and standard TOR-TILD EAM potentials. Compare the free-energy estimates from each method directly with those obtained from full ab initio TI calculations.
measurements: Quantitative free-energy differences from TI calculations
Metrics of phase-space overlap between the reference and ab initio ensembles
Error margins in free-energy predictions (in meV/atom)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid NN-corrected EAM potential fails to reduce the TI path mismatch by at least 30% relative to the TOR-TILD reference, or if the free-energy predictions deviate by more than ±5 meV/atom from the ab initio benchmarks, the hypothesis will be falsified.

frame.system: Multicomponent (high-entropy) alloys in both solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, where the current state involves using EAM (Embedded Atom Method) potentials as references for ab initio liquid configurations.
frame.goal: To devise a single testable methodological intervention that improves the phase-space overlap between the reference (EAM) and target (ab initio) systems, thereby reducing the thermodynamic-integration (TI) path mismatch compared to existing TOR-TILD EAM references.
frame.limitation: The current EAM references are unable to accurately capture the vast array of atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid phase, leading to poor reference–target phase-space overlap and significant thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
root_cause_cues: inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid
reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references
constraints: Intervention must be a single testable methodological change
Must explain why it improves reference–target phase-space overlap
Should predict the quantitative reduction in TI path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references
Must define applicable composition and temperature ranges for high-entropy alloys
Needs to identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations
A decisive free-energy benchmark must be specified to falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: High-temperature regimes at and near the melting point, where both solid and liquid phases of high-entropy alloys are present, ensuring that the method is applicable across the relevant phase transitions.
prior_attempts: TOR-TILD’s EAM references have been used to bridge ab initio and classical descriptions, yet they fall short due to limited configurational diversity in the liquid state.
Standard EAM potentials have been applied in elemental and binary systems but do not extend reliably to the multicomponent complexity of high-entropy alloys at high temperatures.

families.best_lever: Deploy a neural network or Gaussian approximation potential trained on comprehensive ab initio data covering the relevant composition and temperature ranges for high-entropy alloys, ensuring it accurately reproduces the free-energy landscape and reduces TI path mismatch.

families.principle: Improving the accuracy of free-energy integration by enhancing the sampling of phase space, thereby achieving better overlap between the reference and target systems without solely relying on a change in the potential.

levers.lever: Hybrid Neural Network Correction for EAM Potentials
levers.principle: Augment the traditional EAM framework with a neural network that is trained on a diverse dataset (≈10,000 configurations) from ab initio simulations of high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures (typically 0.9–1.1 Tm). This model learns the residual corrections between the standard EAM predictions and ab initio energies, thereby enhancing phase‐space overlap. The neural network refines atomic interactions across solid and liquid regimes, reducing TI path mismatch by an estimated 30–40% relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references. Support comes from similar NN-corrected potentials successfully applied in elemental and binary systems, and a decisive free-energy benchmark would be the ability of the hybrid model to predict free-energy differences within ±5 meV/atom compared to direct ab initio TI calculations.

Use a GPR model to learn a smooth correction term over a strategically sampled set (≈1,000–5,000 configurations) from ab initio datasets covering the high-temperature regime for high-entropy alloys. The GPR’s inherent uncertainty quantification allows targeted sampling in regions of poor EAM performance, hence improving the overall phase-space overlap. This statistical interpolation is expected to reduce the TI integration path mismatch by up to 35% relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references. Elemental and binary alloy studies using GPR in potential fitting provide supporting evidence, and a decisive benchmark is set as achieving a variance in predicted free energies below 10 meV/atom compared to full ab initio integration.

Implement an active learning framework where an initial EAM model is iteratively refined by selectively adding ab initio calculated configurations to the training set (starting with about 500 configurations and adding batches until convergence). This closed-loop system targets the configurations where the model’s prediction error peaks, thereby dynamically enhancing reference–target phase‐space overlap in the ab initio liquid regime. The method is expected to decrease TI path mismatch by roughly 40% compared to TOR-TILD’s references. Successful applications in simpler systems validate the approach, and a decisive free-energy benchmark would be the convergence of TI free-energy differences within ±5 meV/atom over successive active learning iterations.

Employ a VAE to learn a low-dimensional latent representation of the ab initio configuration space from a large dataset (≈10,000 configurations). By sampling from this latent space, one can generate synthetic but physically realistic configurations that expose deficiency areas in the EAM model. These configurations are used to fine-tune the force field, thereby improving phase-space coverage in both liquid and near-melting solid phases. This method is projected to lower the thermodynamic integration mismatch by an estimated 35–45% relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references. Prior use of VAEs in extracting structural features in elemental and binary alloys supports this methodology, and a decisive free-energy benchmark would be a discrepancy of less than 7 meV/atom when comparing TI results from the VAE-enhanced model to direct ab initio calculations.
